1.pericope_label: The word of the Lord that came unto Hosea, the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah
debates: Where the prophet came from and to which kingdom he belonged
How long a ministry the four named reigns imply
Whether a named father indicates a prophetic family
outliers: Clarke reports two rival traditions about the birthplace and parentage and settles neither, while Keil and Delitzsch argue from the dialect of the book itself that its author was a subject of the northern kingdom
Henry dismisses as groundless the conceit that a prophet whose father is named had a prophet for a father
themes: A name meaning saviour, borne by a man who was himself an instrument of saving
A well in a father name, and the living waters prophets draw from
A hundred and twelve years counted between the first and last of the named reigns
A word impressed on the mind, not a fancy or imagination of the prophet own

2.pericope_label: And the Lord said to Hosea, Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms
debates: What the beginning of the word means
Whether the marriage was an event or a vision
Whether the wife was guilty before the marriage or after
outliers: Wesley holds the whole transaction to have been done in vision and proposed as a parable, where Ellicott weighs both theories and comes down for a real marriage
Gill refuses every larger sense of the opening phrase and confines it to the first part of this book
themes: A prophet sent as a herald to proclaim war rather than to exhort
A first message that had to be written and published as a witness
A husband whose wife owed him the fidelity a nation owed its God
Suffering afterwards read back as a command given at the start

3.pericope_label: And the Lord said unto him, Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu
debates: Whether the marriage was carried out or only represented
What the name of the woman signifies
Whether the name of the first child is read for its meaning or for the place it names
outliers: Calvin holds that the prophet never entered a brothel and that figs were laid before the people in place of a wife, against Clarke who calls the whole a real transaction
Keil and Delitzsch reject the sense of destruction in the name of the woman which Gill and Calvin both entertain, and deny that the name of the child is meant to carry its meaning at all
themes: A cake of dried figs standing for a taste for delicacies
A name that sounds almost like the name of the nation itself
A fertile plain that had been the scene of terrible struggles
A bow broken, and with it every arm the kingdom relied on

6.pericope_label: Call her name Lo-ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away
debates: What shade the name of the daughter carries
Why the southern kingdom is exempted here
What deliverance without bow or horsemen refers to
outliers: Calvin denies that the exemption is a verdict on the southern kingdom, citing Isaiah on its drunkenness and impiety and treating the honour as comparison made for the sake of his own hearers
Ellicott hears the despondency of the prophet himself in the name given to the child, where the others read only the sentence on the nation
themes: A daughter cast off and disowned by her father as unworthy of favour
A second name more disgraceful than the first
An army destroyed without bow or sword or horsemen
A covenant dissolved, so that the God of one house is no longer the God of the other

8.pericope_label: Then said God, Call his name Lo-ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God
debates: What the weaning of the second child signifies
Whether the word God belongs in the last clause
How far the third name reaches
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch name Calvin and reject his reading of the weaning as divine patience, taking it instead for the unbroken succession of calamities
Clarke argues from the ancient versions that a word has dropped out of the last clause, though he can point to no manuscript variant supporting it
themes: A child weaned, as a part of the land is taken from the nation
Children of whoredoms carrying the omens their parents earned
Three names in an ascending series, each more grievous than the last
A covenant with the fathers abolished, leaving a people no different from the nations

10.pericope_label: Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered
debates: How the promise of an innumerable seed stands beside the sentence of rejection
Who the children of Israel are in this promise
When the promise was or will be fulfilled
outliers: Gill rejects the fulfilment at the return from captivity, which Theodoret and others held, on the ground that too few came back, and carries it forward to the preaching of the Gospel
Keil and Delitzsch resist reading the promise of all the descendants of Jacob, checking the patriarchal parallel against the clause about those once called not my people
themes: Sand of the sea and stars of heaven, promised to a father long before
A title of the Church claimed as a shield by men alienated from God
The very place where a people were disowned becoming the place where they are owned
A living God who is the fountain of life to his children

11.pericope_label: Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head
debates: When the gathering of the two houses takes place
Who the one head is
What land they are to go up out of
outliers: Ellicott holds that no exile is in view at all and that the land they go up from is their own, taking the phrase as a marching forth to war
Calvin objects that interpreters confound the universal gathering of the previous verse with this address to the natural race of Abraham
themes: Two peoples losing their distinction and passing under one name
A head appointed by the people, recalling a congregation that once appointed one to go back
A curse dropped from the names the children carried
A seed sown among the nations in wrath and reaped in bounty
